 Print Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has expressed his admiration for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after his departure from the AI chip giant, but he also made it clear that any decision about the return of Huang is not his to make. According to a report Fortune, speaking at a media roundtable during Microsoft’s Ignite conference in San Francisco, Nadella described Huang as ‘a singular person’ who has made some significant contributions to both Nvidia and the broader technology industry. However, he stopped short of endorsing a potential comeback for the Nvidia co-founder. "I just want to give him space for what he needs to do there, and it's not up to me. It's up to the Nvidia board to decide what happens next," Nadella said. He added that he has "all the admiration, respect for what Jensen has done for this industry, and what he's done for Nvidia," noting that the two have worked together for many years. Jensen Huang says he is opening to returning to Nvidia as CEO
 Huang stepped down as Nvidia CEO last week amid controversy surrounding revelations about his personal life. The long-time executive, who co-founded Nvidia more than three decades ago and helped transform it into the world's leading AI chipmaker, later said he would be willing to return as CEO if given the opportunity. However, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones subsequently indicated that the company had no plans to bring Huang back to the top role, leaving uncertainty around the executive's future.  Despite Nvidia's leadership turmoil, Nadella expressed confidence in the company's management team and long-term prospects. "Nvidia does have a lot of human capital and very capable leadership," he said, highlighting interim CEO and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, who previously worked at Microsoft. Nadella also stressed the importance of Microsoft's ongoing relationship with the chipmaker, noting that the company is continuing to scale deployment of Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin processors. "I'm making sure that we have the same type of partnership, and we're scaling Rubins as we speak," Nadella said. "It's a pretty critical project for us." Microsoft is one of Nvidia's largest customers, purchasing vast quantities of AI accelerators for its cloud infrastructure. The two companies have maintained a close partnership during the AI boom, with Nadella and Huang frequently appearing together at industry events. Data centre growth depends on community trust
 During the discussion, Nadella also commented on growing opposition to data centre developments across parts of the United States. He said technology companies must earn public trust by demonstrating tangible local benefits rather than relying on lobbying efforts in Washington. According to Nadella, concerns around electricity usage, infrastructure strain and local disruption can only be addressed through long-term engagement with communities. "I don't think the public is getting it wrong," he said, adding that Microsoft's data centre expansion plans remain unchanged despite recent political developments. Nadella noted that the biggest constraints on data centre construction continue to be power availability, chip production capacity and memory supply rather than election outcomes. AI helped Microsoft recover from outage
 The Microsoft chief also addressed the massive Microsoft Outlook outage last week. The service disruption impacted the functioning of Teams, Copilot, SharePoint and other Microsoft 365 services. Nadella emphasised that the service disruption was not caused by any AI-generate code other AI deployments. Instead, he said that it was a ‘perfect story’ in which a software bug emerged during routine testing under specific web traffic conditions. Join conversation

 He further stated that the internal tools at Microsoft actually helped the engineers to diagnose the issue and then resolve the problem. Buyout programme gives employees more choice
 Apart from Huang, Nadella also talked about the recent voluntary buyout offer of Microsoft which was extended to almost 60,000 employees. As per the Microsoft CEO, the programme was aimed to offer more control to the workers over their career decisions instead of leaving them uncertain about the future when it comes to organisational changes. "There are some teams that are changing faster, some teams that are in a different place," Nadella said, referring to the varying pace of transformation across different parts of Microsoft.
